results.title: SSIM vs. LPIPS: Which Metric Should You Trust for Image Quality Evaluation?
results.content: LPIPS: Which Metric Should You Trust for Image Quality Evaluation? Two popular objective metrics often compared in this field are the Structural Similarity Index (SSIM) and Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS). SSIM is a widely used metric that assesses image quality based on the degradation of structural information. The strength of SSIM lies in its ability to model human visual perception by considering image structures. Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity (LPIPS). LPIPS is a more recent metric that takes a machine learning approach to evaluate image quality. Unlike SSIM, LPIPS leverages deep neural networks trained on large datasets to predict human judgments of image similarity. This learned approach allows LPIPS to better model the complexity of human perception by capturing high-level features and textures in images rather than focusing strictly on structural elements. In conclusion, both SSIM and LPIPS serve valuable roles in image quality evaluation, each with their own strengths and weaknesses.

results.title: Perceptual Metrics Face-Off: LPIPS vs SSIM vs PSNR
results.content: # Perceptual Metrics Face-Off: LPIPS vs SSIM vs PSNR. In the realm of image and video quality assessment, perceptual metrics play a pivotal role in understanding how closely a generated image resembles a reference image according to human perception. Among the popular metrics used today are LPIPS (Learned Perceptual Image Patch Similarity), SSIM (Structural Similarity Index), and PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio). Each of these metrics has its unique approach to evaluating image quality, and understanding their differences can offer valuable insights into their applications and limitations. This metric computes the perceptual similarity between two images by comparing their feature representations extracted from a pretrained convolutional neural network. It is particularly effective in tasks where high-level semantic content plays a crucial role, such as in generative adversarial network (GAN) evaluation and image style transfer applications. It evaluates image quality based on structural information, luminance, and contrast. It is computationally efficient and provides a straightforward way to assess image quality, making it a popular choice in various image processing tasks, including compression and denoising. PSNR is perhaps the oldest and most widely recognized metric in image processing. The higher the PSNR, the better the image quality. When comparing LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR, it's essential to consider the context in which each metric excels. SSIM, on the other hand, is useful for applications where preserving structural information is crucial, such as in medical imaging or natural scene analysis. In practical applications, the choice of perceptual metric can significantly influence the outcome of image quality assessments. For instance, in video streaming services, where bandwidth constraints necessitate compression, SSIM might be preferred for maintaining structural quality, while LPIPS could be useful for ensuring the perceptual richness of streamed content. SSIM, while robust, may not capture perceptual nuances that LPIPS can, and PSNR’s lack of consideration for human perception means it can be misleading in assessing perceptual quality. In conclusion, LPIPS, SSIM, and PSNR each offer unique perspectives on image quality assessment. While no single metric can universally capture the complexity of human perception, a combination or careful selection of these metrics can provide a more comprehensive evaluation framework for image processing tasks.

results.content: # Bootstrap vs other simulated data methods. In the mixed effect model, many statisticians would like to simulate or bootstrap data to create empirical confidence regions for fixed effect parameters and random effect parameters. $\begingroup$ I don't understand your question. You mention a model and simulating to estimate but don't mention data? Bootstrap requires resampling from the original data and bootstrap is not the same as Monte Carlo on the empirical distribution. If you have data and you don't want to rely on Gaussian assumptions bootstrapping the data using the Monte Carlo approximation is possible. $\begingroup$ You would do that I think if you had a parametric model but no data and wanted to see what a data set from a mixed model would look like under those assumptions. When you have some data you bootstrap, when you don't you simulate multivariate data. * $\begingroup$ If I make it a question would you upvote and give it an accept? To bootstrap in a mixed effects linear model you would do sampling with replacement in a way that maintains the model structure. Once you have done this you have a bootstrap sample. You fit the model to this bootstrap sample and then repeat the bootstrapping followed by model fitting many times. Any time you have a bootstrap histogram of estimates you can construct bootstrap confidence intervals from this collection of estimates. The simplest is Efron's percentile method which takes the 2.5 percentile and the 97.5 percentile from these ordered bootstrap estimate to be the endpoint of a 95% confidence interval. Now in the absence of data you may want to get an understanding of how the model works. then you can do simulation of the data and look at the results in a way similar to what I described for the bootstrap. results.content: # How to bootstrap the AUC on a data-set with 50,000 entries? I do have AUC-ROC curve of the data-set. How should I proceed to bootstrap the AUC? If I do the sampling of the same size as data-set then my AUC value would not be the same all the time? * $\begingroup$ AUC is area under the ROC curve, but it's also a property of a classifier's classification, not the data. What do you mean by bootstrap and what does it mean to take a sample of a data set that's the same size as the data set? I did find the AUC of ROC curve for different threshold probabilities/decision boundaries. The value of AUC I found for the data-set is close to 0.77. ## 3 Answers 3. Yes, sample the same size of your data set (with replacement), then find your AUC, say 10,000 times. When you sample with replacement, you will only find around 63% of the entries in your new bootstrapped data set will be unique (so many of these will have 2+ identical entries in the bootstrapped data set. 4) Now you have 10,000 AUCs. If you take the 5th percentile and 95th percentile, you have the bootstrapped 95% confidence interval. Rather than just doing one AUC calculation on your full data and saying the AUC is $.77$, you may end up finding your AUC is $.75 +/- .03$, which is much more reliable to make a claim on. answered Oct 5, 2016 at 12:19. results.title: 이미지/비디오 품질 평가 지표 (PSNR, SSIM, MOS, LPIPS)
results.content: # 이미지/비디오 품질 평가 지표 (PSNR, SSIM, MOS, LPIPS). * PSNR은 원본 이미지와 복원된 이미지 간 **픽셀 차이**를 기반으로 품질 측정하는 지표임. * SSIM은 **구조적 유사성**을 기반으로 품질 평가하는 지표임. > * SSIM은 0에서 1 사이의 값을 가지며, 1에 가까울수록 두 이미지가 더 비슷함. > * PSNR에 비해 더 직관적으로 품질 평가 가능. ### PSNR vs SSIM 비교. > * PSNR: 모델 학습 중 품질 비교에 적합함. > * SSIM: 사용자 경험을 더 잘 반영하는 품질 평가에 적합함. ### **표시된 PSNR / SSIM 값**. * PSNR / SSIM 없음 (원본이므로 비교 기준). * SRResNet이 가장 높은 PSNR(23.53dB)을 기록함. 이는 픽셀 간 차이를 줄이는 데 SRResNet이 더 잘 작동했음을 의미함. * SRGAN은 PSNR(21.15dB)이 Bicubic(21.59dB)보다 낮음. 이는 SRGAN이 PSNR 최적화 대신 **시각적 품질**(디테일 복원)에 집중했기 때문임. * SRGAN은 SSIM(0.6868)이 Bicubic(0.6423)보다 약간 나은 수준. 이는 SRGAN이 **사람이 느끼는 품질**에 더 초점을 맞춘 모델임을 나타냄. > * **PSNR/SSIM** 지표만 보면 SRResNet이 더 나은 성능을 보임. > * 하지만 **시각적 품질** 측면에서는 SRGAN이 더 좋은 디테일 복원을 보여줌. > * **PSNR과 SSIM은 정량적 평가 지표**이며, SRGAN처럼 시각적 품질이 중요한 경우 **MOS**나 **LPIPS** 같은 평가가 더 적합할 수 있음. > MOS는 **주관적인 품질 평가 지표**로, 사람이 직접 이미지를 보고 평가한 결과를 평균낸 값임. 주로 이미지나 비디오 품질의 **시각적 품질**을 평가할 때 사용됨. * 디테일 복원, 자연스러움, 색감 등 **시각적 품질**에 더 민감한 평가. > MOS는 PSNR이나 SSIM 같은 정량적 지표로는 평가하기 어려운 **시각적 디테일**과 **자연스러움**을 측정하는 데 유용함. > GAN 기반 모델(SRGAN, ESRGAN 등)은 MOS 점수를 높이는 데 초점이 맞춰짐. ### **MOS vs PSNR/SSIM**. > LPIPS는 **딥러닝 기반으로 시각적 품질을 평가하는 지표**로, 두 이미지 간의 유사성을 측정. 인간이 느끼는 시각적 품질과 유사한 기준으로 설계되었으며, 특히 **GAN 기반 모델 평가**에서 널리 사용. * LPIPS는 두 이미지의 특징(feature)을 딥러닝 모델(예: VGG, AlexNet 등)로 추출한 뒤, 이 특징 간의 유사성을 비교함. * 단순히 픽셀 차이를 보는 PSNR과 달리, 이미지의 **고차원적 시각적 특징**을 평가함. * LPIPS 값은 **0~1 사이**이며, 0에 가까울수록 두 이미지가 더 유사함. * PSNR/SSIM처럼 수학적으로 계산되지만, **시각적 품질과 더 밀접하게 관련됨**. ### **LPIPS vs PSNR/SSIM**. > 이 네 가지는 모두 이미지 및 비디오 품질 평가 지표로 사용 가능함. > * **정량적 비교**가 필요하면 PSNR, SSIM 사용. > 특정 상황에 따라 **PSNR + SSIM + MOS/LPIPS**를 **조합하여 활용**하는 것이 최적의 방법임.
